passage:
After Friday prayers, Irfan and Abhinav took their tea to the low wall by the corner stall.
"You told me last week you don't get some of the rules," Abhinav said. "So why go every Friday?"
"Because it's home. Rahim Uncle saves my spot. The boys are there. Ammi's sheer khurma on Eid. When I was small, the smell of that carpet meant safe."
"And the questions?"
"I ask them. I asked our imam about one thing and he said, 'Good question, come Sunday and we'll talk.' He wasn't angry."
"So you don't have to pick."
Irfan turned the glass in his hands. "I keep waiting to be afraid of picking. I'm just not."

qa.q: Who saves Irfan's spot at the mosque?
What is Irfan feeling toward the mosque, and what shows it?
qa.a: Irfan feels belonging and warmth, shown by "it's home" and the memory of the carpet smelling safe, while still holding real questions.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend who wants both belonging and questions?
qa.a: Keep going to the place that feels like home, and ask the questions to an elder or friend who welcomes them, without fearing either.

qa.q: How does Abhinav see Irfan's stance?
qa.a: With curiosity; Abhinav asks why Irfan goes despite the doubts and ends up saying Irfan does not have to pick.

grounding: Irfan finds friends and a sense of home at the mosque and still asks questions, keeping both without fear.

passage:
Temple kitchen volunteer coordinator's note, Sunday seva

Uma has been coming to the Sunday kitchen every week since she was twelve. She stirs the sambar pot, knows every volunteer aunty by name, and this year she brought her school friend Zainab, who now chops vegetables beside her. The two of them laugh the whole morning.

Today, after serving, Uma asked the priest why only men could carry the deity in procession. A few people looked uneasy. The priest answered calmly, as far as he could. Uma listened and nodded. Later she told me, "I love it here. It feels like home. But I also want to understand the reasons, not just follow."

She seemed worried that asking made her a bad devotee. I told her many people here have asked questions over the years, and still come. The kitchen is not only for people who never ask anything.

She went back and washed the big vessels with Zainab until two. I have asked the priest if the youth group could hold a question session next month.

qa.q: What does Uma stir at the Sunday kitchen?
What was Uma worried about after asking the priest her question?
qa.a: Uma was worried and uneasy that asking questions made her a bad devotee, even though the temple feels like home.

qa.q: How did the coordinator help Uma keep both belonging and questions?
qa.a: The coordinator told Uma that many people have asked questions and still come, and asked the priest about a question session for the youth group.

qa.q: How might Zainab see Uma's place at the temple kitchen?
qa.a: Zainab likely sees how much at home Uma feels, laughing with her all morning, and may admire that Uma feels free to ask questions.

grounding: It shows a teen who finds friends and a sense of home at the temple, values that belonging, and also asks questions without fearing either.

passage:
Sunday, 9 pm

Langar seva again today. I love Sundays at the gurdwara. Vishal and I did the roti line for three hours, flour up to our elbows, and Bebe ji from the next street kept slipping us extra kheer. It's the one place where everyone knows me since I was a baby.

But today I asked Granthi ji something I've been thinking about for months, why some families still sit apart even though the Guru taught equality. My voice shook. I was sure he'd be annoyed.

He wasn't. He said, "Good. The Guru asked questions too," and told me about a book I could read.

On the way home Vishal said, "Weren't you scared?" I was. I'm always scared someone will say asking means I don't belong. But I think I can have both, the roti line and the questions. They don't cancel each other out.

— Urmila

qa.q: What did Urmila and Vishal do in the langar for three hours?
qa.a: They did the roti line for three hours.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling before Granthi ji answered?
qa.a: Urmila felt nervous, with a shaking voice, sure that the question would annoy him.

qa.q: What helped Urmila keep both belonging and questions?
qa.a: Granthi ji welcomed the question and suggested a book, which showed Urmila that asking did not mean leaving the community.

qa.q: What might Vishal think about Urmila's question?
qa.a: Vishal seems surprised by Urmila's courage, perhaps expecting that asking questions at the gurdwara would cause trouble.

grounding: It shows a teen who finds friends and home at the gurdwara, values that belonging and also asks questions without fearing either.
